# Sourdough Hydration Table

## Overview

Hydration is the water weight divided by the flour weight, written as a percentage, and it is the single number that decides how a dough behaves on the bench. I keep a table on the cupboard door so I stop doing the arithmetic mid-mix. It is built on 1000 g of flour, with a second column for a smaller 500 g mix.

| Hydration | Water for 1000 g flour | Water for 500 g flour | What it handles |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 65% | 650 g | 325 g | Sandwich loaves and stiff enriched doughs that need to hold a tin |
| 70% | 700 g | 350 g | Everyday white loaves and bagels, easy to shape |
| 75% | 750 g | 375 g | Open-crumb country loaves, my usual bake |
| 80% | 800 g | 400 g | Ciabatta-style doughs and wholemeal blends that soak up water |
| 85% | 850 g | 425 g | High-extraction flour and wet doughs handled with a bench scraper |

The low end is for loaves that must stand up in a tin, and the high end is for flour that keeps asking for more water. Between them sits most of what I bake.

## Notes

The table is a starting point, not a rule. Wholemeal flour is thirsty because the bran and the germ soak up water that white flour leaves free, so a blend with a third of it will take another five to ten per cent hydration and still feel stiff. I add the extra water slowly, in splashes, and I stop when the dough stops looking ragged. Rye is the extreme case: it drinks water far past what the table suggests and it never develops the same gluten, so I read the bowl rather than the number.

I read the dough rather than the percentage as the mix goes on. A dough at 75% that was measured carefully can still feel dry if the flour is fresh from a cold cupboard, and one at 70% can feel slack on a humid day. The signs matter more than the figure: the dough should clear the side of the bowl on the final mix, feel tacky rather than sticky, and hold a soft shape after a fold. If it spreads the moment I let go, the hydration is too high for that flour, and I fold in a spoon of flour rather than pressing on.

Starters and salt bend the numbers too. A wet starter adds water as well as flour, so a 100% starter counts for half its weight as each, and I adjust the final water to keep the dough where I want it. Salt tightens the gluten, so a dough that feels loose before the salt often feels right after it. I mix the flour and water first, rest the dough for a while, then add the salt, and I judge the texture again at that point.

Finally I keep the same flour and the same starter for a month before I change anything, so the table stays meaningful. A new bag of flour is a new set of numbers, and I would rather learn one flour well than chase five of them badly.

## Troubleshooting

A dough that feels like porridge at a hydration I have managed before usually means the flour is weaker than the last bag, so I knead a little longer and add flour in small spoons. A dough that tears instead of stretching is under-hydrated for that flour, so I add water a spoon at a time. A loaf that comes out dense and damp is often proofed too long rather than mixed too wet, so I shorten the bulk next time. Sticky dough that sticks to everything is a sign to wet my hands rather than add flour, because extra flour changes the very percentage I was trying to hit. If the crumb is tight when I wanted it open, I raise the hydration by five points and fold more gently, and if the loaf spreads in the oven I drop it by five and shape tighter. A dough that feels right but bakes flat usually needs a longer bulk rather than less water, and one that bakes dense needs less. When two changes confuse the result, I hold everything else still and change one number at a time, because the table is only useful if I can tell which column is doing the work.
